title: Race on opposite wings
summary: Advance the a-pawn toward the white king, but watch White's kingside attack.

fromNode.nodeId: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6

goal: Create queenside pressure while keeping enough time to meet White's attack.

steps.text: In the example, the kings are on opposite wings. White has a pawn on h5 near your king, so check the kingside before advancing.
In the example, the a-pawn can advance to a5 and then a4. Each move needs a fresh calculation.
In the example, the pawn can reach a3 and attack b2. If it captures on b2, the rook gains a half-open a-file.
The file and the pawn do not guarantee mate. White can attack quickly too; be ready to defend or choose a central move instead.
In the trap example, if White takes the b2 pawn with the king, the rook can move to a3 and attack the queen. The e7 bishop defends the rook. White has a stronger reply than taking the pawn.

jobs.text: The a-pawn can advance toward the white king.
The rook can use the a-file if the a-pawn leaves it.
The c-pawn controls b5 and d5.
Your king must be protected against White's kingside play.

breaks.text: The a-pawn can advance toward the white king.

opponent.text: White can bring a rook to the g-file and advance the g-pawn. Calculate the threats before another pawn move.

notNow: Do not continue the pawn advance if you must answer a check or a direct threat to your king.
The example is a race, not a forced win. A central move can also be strong.

mistakes.text: The pawn on b2 can capture a bishop that goes to a3. Advance the pawn instead.

comments.text: The a-pawn starts toward White's queenside.
The pawn on a3 attacks b2.
The a-pawn captures on b2, leaving the a-file half open for the rook.

models.title: Trap: the rook attacks the queen

comments.text: This king capture is a mistake; White has stronger moves.
